studies.label: Online experiment: printer-uses writing task with vs without ChatGPT

counts_source.quote: Forty-three people who failed the attention check were excluded from further analysis, leaving a final sample of 225.

arms.name: AI
arms.description: Participants were explicitly asked to make sure they used ChatGPT for the task; use was reported after completion (PDF p. 5, Section 2.2).

arms.name: Control
arms.description: Participants were forbidden from using ChatGPT for the task and reported any tools used after completion (PDF p. 5, Section 2.2).

studies.task: Write a short piece proposing as many unique uses as possible for a hypothetical printer that can print anything, while minimizing grammar errors and maximizing clarity.

ai_tool.name: ChatGPT (participant model and tier not stated)
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 5, Section 2.2 (assigned tool); PDF p. 1, Introduction (product release year): Since its release on November 30, 2022, ChatGPT, a generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), has become a major platform, acquiring users at an unprecedented rate.

preregistration.where: Open Science Framework: https://osf.io/dt5up?mode=&revisionId=&view_only= (PDF pp. 12–13, Pre-registration; also PDF p. 4, Section 2.1).

estimates.outcome: Frequency (fluency): different uses of the printer per participant
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Counts from each participant’s submitted piece, automatically coded using a few-shot LLM prompt. The paper names GPT4o and GPT4 Turbo, but does not identify which model supplied the analyzed counts. The procedure was validated against blinded human raters on a subset; the analysis is not a human creativity rating. Measure is category_count because the scored quantities are uses and conceptual categories (PDF p. 5, Section 2.3).

sources.quote: Fluency (quantity of ideas) indicated by the total number of different uses of the printer

participants who used ChatGPT were more likely to perform better across all aspects of the task, including higher frequency and flexibility of creativity, less inaccuracy and unclarity from their writing

estimates.notes: The full-sample AI-versus-Control contrast is described in PDF pp. 5–6, Sections 3.1–3.2, but its coefficient, SE, p-value, arm means and SDs are not printed in the available PDF. The paper refers to SI Table 3, which is not on file. Fig. 2 shows subgroup means and confidence intervals without numerical labels; no values were read from plotted positions and no subgroups were combined. The study-level final sample is reported, but outcome-specific analysis counts and arm counts are not printed; estimate counts remain null.

participants who used ChatGPT were more likely to perform better across all aspects of the task, including higher frequency and flexibility of creativity, less inaccuracy and unclarity from their writing

estimates.notes: The full-sample AI-versus-Control contrast is described in PDF pp. 5–6, Sections 3.1–3.2, but its coefficient, SE, p-value, arm means and SDs are not printed in the available PDF. open_items: SI Tables 1–6 are referenced but no supplement file is present in the retrieval entry, supplement manifest, or beside the source PDF. In particular, SI Table 3 is needed for the full-sample frequency, flexibility, inaccuracy, and unclarity coefficients, SEs, and any reported arm summaries.

The number randomized and the AI and Control arm counts are not printed. The study reports 266 completions, exclusion of forty-three people, and a final sample of 225 (PDF p. 4); these printed counts are inconsistent. The stated final sample is retained only at study level. Exact counts for each extracted outcome analysis are unconfirmed and remain null; no counts were derived from degrees of freedom.

The text on PDF p. 7 reverses the group-level outcome labels relative to Fig. 5 on PDF p. 9. Records follow the figure panel labels and screening decision while preserving the contradictory text verbatim. The caption also reverses the wording about ChatGPT use. SI Table 5 or author clarification would resolve the publication errors.

The construction of the group-level counts is not specified: whether duplicates across people were removed, how conceptual domains were pooled, and whether unequal arm sizes were accounted for. No full-sample uncertainty for these set-level measures is printed.

The paper does not identify the ChatGPT model or tier used by participants, how they accessed it, or any instructions on the manner of use beyond requiring ChatGPT. The recorded year is the ChatGPT product release year explicitly stated in the introduction, not a model-year inference.
GPT4o and GPT4 Turbo are named as scoring models, but which model supplied the final analyzed counts is not specified (PDF p. 5, Section 2.3).
The paper reports preregistration but does not identify a preregistered primary outcome. The preregistration could not be inspected, so primary-outcome fields remain null or not_stated.

The paper labels participants by English proficiency and prior ChatGPT experience before individual randomization but does not explicitly state whether randomization was stratified by those groups (PDF pp. 4–5).
notes: Extracted by B on 2026-10-10. The complete markdown conversion was read in chunks, including the appendix and references. All figures were visually inspected by rendering the PDF in memory; the source pages for every retained number and quotation were checked with pymupdf. PDF page indexes plus one match the printed page numbers. No tables were detected in the main results pages; all statistical tables are referenced as SI. Full-sample output-statistic inventory: the prose prints the two condition-level pairs 635 versus 552 and 442 versus 313; no numerical full-sample individual-outcome coefficient, mean, SD, SE, test, p-value, or interval appears in the available PDF. The four individual-outcome records therefore retain the reported contrasts with null statistics. The two set-level records use the prose numbers with the Fig. 5 outcome labels, and do not use estimated plot coordinates. Grammar-error and clarity-suggestion counts are retained as other output outcomes from the divergent-thinking task, not as creativity effects. There is no later unassisted creative-output task. The screening form reports no known shared sample. No supplement was read: direct urllib requests to the named ScienceDirect article, OSF registration API, and Oxford repository record all failed with a local socket-permission error (WinError 10013). Requests used User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1 and no personal identifier. No external data or documents were saved, no statistics were computed, and only this extraction file was written.
